doc.title: Ken Poston interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2024

title: Interviewing Count Basie backstage as a high school student
summary: As a teen he interviewed Basie at the Uptown Theater; Basie deflected until Poston mentioned playing Sammy Nestico charts, and Poston learned credibility with musicians matters.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Count Basie was coming to Kansas City and because we had played all those Sammy Nestico charts in the high school band, I knew who — Count Basie, I’d read about Count Basie and the connection to Kansas City that I thought for the school newspaper I was going to write a big history of Kansas City jazz and this would be great if I could interview Count Basie then that could be a part of my Kansas City jazz history and it’d be really great in high school to be able to do that. So our principal knew somebody and was able to get it set up for me to interview Count Basie backstage at the Uptown Theater. That would have been 1978 or 1979, somewhere in there. And of course I was scared to death and I made my questions up, I had five or six questions, and I knew I only had about ten minutes with him or whatever it was. So I get there and they’ve got all the journalists who, everybody but me was like a real journalist. And I’m sitting there, got my suit on and I got my little tape recorder and the microphone and I’m terrified that the mic is not going to work or whatever the case may be. But there’s I don’t know six or seven other journalists there that are all set up to interview. So they’re not there yet, but I’ll never forget, the stage door swings open and the Basie band starts coming in. And I’m sitting right there. And all of a sudden Freddie Green walks in. And I knew, I’d done my homework enough, I knew who all these guys were, and here’s Freddie Green. And all of a sudden this reality comes over me about oh my God that’s Freddie Green, I have to interview — thinking I can’t do this, and so I’m starting to get really scared once I saw Freddie Green. And then Basie comes in. And Basie comes in, everybody’s clapping, he’s got the captain’s hat and the cigar going, and they put him in this room and I’m thinking to myself okay, well I can pull myself together, look at my questions, there’s all these other journalists so give me some time to get together. Of course I’m the first one called. Immediately they called me. So I go in and I asked my first question which was so — these were all very pedestrian questions. You know, “What was the Kansas City jazz scene like when you were —” something like that. First thing out of Basie’s mouth,

which I heard him do many other times but I didn’t know this at the time but I heard him do this in many other interviews, “Oh well you see I’m writing a book. I’m writing my biography, and I can’t talk about those things that are going to be in the book, so you got any more questions? And of course you can imagine like a 16-, 17-year-old kid that has — and I don’t know what to do. So I kind of re-phrased the question. I guess I don’t know what I said but I kind of re-phrased it. And then Basie goes, “You know that’s kind of the same question.” And I go oh well — “What about Lester Young?” Lester Young. “Yeah, Lester Young was a stylist.” That’s all he said. I’m, oh, so I’m running out of my questions and I’m not sure what to do. So finally I just start winging it, ‘cause I see this isn’t going to work and it scared me when he wouldn’t answer the question. So I just said, “Well,” I said, “thanks” I said, “I just wanted to tell you you know my high — I’m in my high school band and we don’t play anything — we play all the Sammy Nestico charts. The minute I said that his whole demeanor changed, and he just became — he was so thrilled you know. “Oh you play my music?” I’m like, “Yeah we play ‘Wind Machine’ and this and this and this. He’s like, “Oh” he goes, “man” he goes, “I would sure like to hear you guys.” I said, “Well” you know, “you should come over to my school.” He goes, “I will, next time I’m in town you get a hold of me and I’ll come over and hear you guys.” And it never happened but I was able to take the tape back and play it for everybody and everybody’s like, “Oh my God.” So then after that he started answering my questions. So I ended up getting some stuff from him because all of a sudden, and that taught me kind of an interesting thing too is that the way that the musicians view you makes all the difference in the world. If you gain credibility with them, which often you have to do I think — I think what’s helped me through the years is having the music background has helped me and in some ways separated me from some other people who do what I do, certainly not everybody. But I’m able to speak that language, and also then in doing the interviews I speak a language where I can ask certain questions that — and I realized, and I don’t know if I realized it right at that moment or not, but gaining the respect of the musicians and gaining credibility opens many avenues for you with the musicians that you might not get if they just kind of write you off as, you know, somebody who doesn’t know or hasn’t done their homework or really didn’t. So but that’s the Basie story. Real quickly you could — I’ll real quickly tell you a fast Jay McShann funny thing from when I was in Kansas City. Jay and I went to lunch about once a week when I was working at the Kansas City Jazz Commission. There were places Jay liked to go, I think there was food he wasn’t supposed to be eating but I never — I’d pick him up and we’d go wherever he wanted to go: Gates & Sons, and Arthur Bryant’s, or wherever it may be. There was Ruby’s Soul Food not too far from where my office was, and we went to Ruby’s Soul Food. And we’re sitting having lunch and this woman,
